key_insight: Time-resolved 4D velocity measurements reveal that laminar thermal plumes in high-Prandtl-number convection do not simply rise independently, but evolve through repeated interactions such as merging, splitting, branching, pulsing, and detachment.
engineering_relevance: These results provide a quantitative benchmark for modeling plume-laden convection in mantle dynamics and other high-viscosity thermal transport systems where multi-plume interactions control heat transfer and material transport.
method: Performed time-resolved volumetric velocity measurements in a high-Prandtl-number Rayleigh-Bénard convection experiment with temperature-dependent viscosity.
Tracked tens of coexisting plumes in 4D to measure morphology, spacing, initiation timing, and interaction pathways over time.
Compared observed plume statistics and length/time scales against prior theoretical and experimental plume studies.
evidence_signal: The abstract reports 4D experimental observations of tens of plumes and quantifies that the fraction of isolated plumes varies from 0–60% as the flow evolves.
watch_item: The findings come from an experimental analogue of mantle convection, so direct extrapolation to Earth-scale conditions depends on how well the laboratory viscosity, boundary layers, and forcing match natural settings.
paper_title: Morphology, interactions, and evolution of laminar thermal plumes revealed by time-resolved volumetric velocity measurements and analysis: Application to Earth's mantle
